p.src: Now the Great King Who Surpasses the Year had barred every gate, front and rear, and ordered a search for the Pilgrim; the uproar continued until dusk, but no trace of him was found. Seated in the Skinning Pavilion, he assembled the demons and issued his commands, ordering the guards at every gate to ring bells and call the watch, beat drums and strike clappers; every one of them strung his bow, drew his blade, and kept watch through the night.

p.src: As it happened, Great Sage Sun had changed himself into a foolish little bluebottle and was clinging beside the door. Seeing how tightly the front was guarded, he spread his wings and flew to the entrance of the rear palace, where he saw the Lady of the Golden Sage lying across the imperial table, shedding clear tears and quietly grieving. The Pilgrim flew through the door and gently alighted on her loosened cloud-dark hair to hear what she was lamenting. After a while, the lady suddenly cried aloud, “My lord, you and I—”

p.src: On hearing this, the Pilgrim moved behind her ear and whispered, “Lady of the Sacred Palace, do not be afraid. I am still Elder Sun, the holy monk sent here by your kingdom, and I have not been killed. It was only because of my own impatience that I stole the golden bells near the dressing table; while you were drinking with the demon king, I slipped privately out of the front pavilion and could not resist opening them for a look. Unexpectedly, I tugged loose the cotton plugs, and when the bells rang once, smoke, fire, and yellow sand burst forth. I panicked and dropped the golden bells, resumed my true form, and fought desperately with my iron staff, but could not break out. Fearing I might fall victim to his deadly hand, I changed into a little fly, clung to the door hinge, and have hidden there until now. The demon king has tightened security still further and refuses to open the gates. Treat him once more as a wife treats her husband and coax him inside to sleep. Then I can act and escape, and devise another way to rescue you.”

p.src: When the lady heard these words, she trembled all over, her hair standing on end as though seized by a spirit; weak with terror, her heart pounded as though struck by a pestle. Her eyes brimming with tears, she asked, “Are you now a man or a ghost?” The Pilgrim replied, “I am neither man nor ghost; I have now changed myself into a little fly and am here beside you. Do not be afraid. Go quickly and invite the demon king here.” The lady did not believe him and, weeping, whispered softly, “Do not haunt my dreams and bewitch me.” The Pilgrim said, “How would I dare bewitch you? If you do not believe me, open your hand and let me jump down for you to see.” The lady truly opened her left hand, and the Pilgrim gently flew down. He landed in her jade-white palm, looking just like this:

p.src: The Lady of the Golden Sage raised her jade-white palm high and called, “Holy monk!” The Pilgrim buzzed in reply, “I am the holy monk transformed.” Only then did the lady believe him. She whispered, “When I invite the demon king here, how will you act?” The Pilgrim said, “The ancients said, ‘Nothing ruins a whole life like wine.’ They also said, ‘Nothing surpasses wine for undoing every affair.’ Wine has uses of many kinds; you need only make drinking your chief device. Call in one of your personal maids and point her out to me. I shall assume her appearance and wait at your side, which will give me the perfect chance to strike.”

p.src: The lady followed his advice and called, “Where is Chunjiao?” From behind the screen emerged a fair-faced vixen, who knelt and asked, “What command has Your Ladyship for Chunjiao?” The lady said, “Tell them to light the gauze lanterns and burn borneol and musk. Help me to the front court so I may invite the king to retire for the night.” Chunjiao went to the front at once and summoned seven or eight deer and fox demons, who formed ranks to either side bearing two pairs of lanterns and a pair of censers. The lady rose slightly and folded her hands, while the Great Sage had already flown away. That splendid Pilgrim spread his wings, flew straight onto the fair-faced vixen’s head, plucked out one of his hairs, breathed immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It changed into a sleep-inducing insect, which he gently placed on her face. Now when a sleep-inducing insect lands on someone’s face, it crawls toward the nostrils; once it enters, the person immediately falls asleep. Sure enough, Chunjiao gradually grew drowsy. Unable to stay on her feet, she swayed and nodded, then hurried back to her usual sleeping place, dropped her head, and began snoring soundly. The Pilgrim jumped down, shook himself, and changed into Chunjiao’s exact likeness. He went around the screen and took his place in the ranks with the others; of this we shall say no more for now.

p.src: Meanwhile, as the Lady of the Golden Sage was walking toward the front, a young demon saw her and reported to the Great King Who Surpasses the Year, “Great King, the lady is coming.” The demon king hurried out beyond the Skinning Pavilion to welcome her. The lady said, “Great King, now that the smoke and fire have died away and the thief has vanished without trace, I have come at this late hour especially to invite you to retire.” The demon was delighted and said, “My lady, take good care. That thief just now was none other than Sun Wukong. He defeated my vanguard, killed my junior officers, and used his transformations to enter and deceive us. Though we have searched like this, he has vanished without a trace, and so my heart remains uneasy.” The lady said, “That rogue must have escaped. Set your mind at ease, Great King, and trouble yourself no further. Come and rest.” Seeing the lady standing respectfully before him and earnestly inviting him, the demon could not persist in refusing. He merely instructed the host of demons to take care with the lamps and fires and guard closely against thieves, then went directly with the lady toward the rear palace. The Pilgrim, disguised as Chunjiao, entered among the two files of attending maids.

p.src: The lady ordered, “Prepare wine to relieve the Great King’s weariness.” The demon king laughed and said, “Just so, just so. Bring the wine quickly, and I shall drink with my lady to settle our nerves.” The false Chunjiao and the other demons laid out fruit, prepared some raw and bloody meat, and arranged the tables and chairs. The lady raised a cup, and the demon king offered one in return; the two exchanged their wine cups. Standing beside them with the winepot, the false Chunjiao said, “Great King and my lady, only tonight have you exchanged nuptial cups. Please drain them both and make it a double cup of joy.” They did indeed have their cups refilled and drained them again. The “false Chunjiao” said again, “The Great King and the lady are joyfully united. Let the maids who can sing offer songs, and those who dance well begin to dance.” Before she had finished speaking, a chorus of song arose; all followed the melody, some singing and others dancing. After the two had drunk a great deal more, the lady ordered the singing and dancing to cease. The attending maids divided into two ranks and formed lines outside the screen. Only the false Chunjiao remained with the winepot, serving wine first to one and then the other. The lady and the demon king spoke only of matters between husband and wife. Just see how the lady feigned a whole world of amorous tenderness, beguiling the demon king until his bones softened and his sinews went numb. Yet he lacked the good fortune ever to touch her body. Pitiful indeed! It was truly like a cat biting a pig’s bladder—an empty delight.

p.src: After they had talked and laughed for a while, the lady asked, “Your Majesty, was the treasure damaged?” The demon king replied, “This treasure was forged from the primal substance of Heaven; how could it be damaged? It is only that the thief pulled out the wad that stopped its mouth and burned the leopard-skin bundle.” The lady said, “Then how did you put it away?” The demon king replied, “There was no need to put it away. I am carrying it at my waist.” On hearing this, the false Chunjiao plucked out a handful of hairs and chewed them to pieces. Edging gently toward the demon king, she placed the hairs upon him, breathed three breaths of immortal breath over them, and secretly cried, “Change!” The hairs at once changed into three kinds of vermin—lice, fleas, and bedbugs—which burrowed into the demon king’s clothes and bit wildly wherever they touched his skin. The demon king could not endure the maddening itch. He thrust a hand inside his robe to feel and scratch, pinched out several lice, and held them near the lamp to inspect them. Seeing this, the lady suppressed a smile and said, “Your Majesty, your underclothes must have grown dirty from going so long without washing and starching; that is why these creatures have appeared.” The demon king said in embarrassment, “I have never had such things before. Of all nights, I must disgrace myself tonight.” The lady laughed. “Why should Your Majesty be disgraced? As the saying goes, ‘Even an emperor has three imperial lice upon him.’ Take off your clothes and let me pick them out for you.” The demon king truly did undo his sash and remove his clothes.

p.src: Standing beside him, the false Chunjiao watched the demon king’s clothes closely. Fleas were leaping in every layer, and great bedbugs lined every garment; lice large and small swarmed thickly together, like mole crickets and ants pouring from a nest. By the time the third layer had inadvertently been opened to expose his flesh, countless vermin were also swarming over the golden bells. The false Chunjiao said, “Your Majesty, give me the bells and let me pick the lice off them too.” The demon king was both ashamed and flustered, and could not distinguish true from false, so he handed the three bells to the false Chunjiao. The false Chunjiao took them and made a show of examining them for some time. When she saw the demon king lowering his head to shake out his clothes, she hid the golden bells, plucked out a hair, changed it into three bells identical to the originals, and held them before the lamp as if inspecting them. Then she twisted and wriggled her body and gave it a shake, recalling the lice, bedbugs, and fleas to herself, before handing the false golden bells back to the monster. The monster took them, still utterly confused and helpless. Unable to tell true from false, he held the bells in both hands and passed them to the lady, saying, “This time put them away properly. Be very, very careful, and do not let what happened before happen again.” The lady took them, gently opened her clothes chest, put away the false bells, and secured it with a golden lock. After drinking several more cups of wine with the demon king, she ordered her maids, “Clean the ivory bed and spread out the brocade quilt. The king and I shall sleep together.” The demon king repeatedly demurred, “I am not so blessed, not so blessed! I dare not share your bed. I shall take a palace maid and sleep in the western palace. My lady, please retire by yourself.” Thus they each retired to their own sleeping quarters, and nothing more need be said of it.

p.src: Now the false Chunjiao, having succeeded, fastened the treasure at his waist, resumed his true form, shook himself, recalled the drowsiness insect, and went straight ahead. He heard the watchman’s clapper and bell sounding together, urgently striking the third watch. Fine Monkey! He formed a hand seal, recited a spell, and worked an invisibility magic. Going straight to the gate, he found it securely barred and locked. He took out the gold-banded staff, pointed it at the gate, and used the lock-opening spell. The gate quietly swung open. He hurried through, planted himself outside, and shouted sternly, “Sai Taisui, give Lady Golden Sage back to me!” He shouted two or three times, alarming every demon great and small. When they hurried to look, they found the front gate open. They hastily lit lamps, found the lock, and secured the gate again. Several were sent running inside to report, “Your Majesty, someone outside the main gate is calling Your Majesty by name and demanding Lady Golden Sage.” A palace maid came out through the palace gate and quietly passed on the word: “Do not make such a racket. His Majesty has only just fallen asleep.” Monkey shouted again before the gate, but the lesser demons did not dare disturb their king. This happened three or four times, yet none dared go in to report. The Great Sage kept clamoring and making an uproar outside until daybreak. At last he lost patience, swung his iron staff, and went forward to batter the gate. In panic, the demons great and small rushed about, some bracing the gate and others carrying word inside. The demon king had only just awakened. Hearing the turmoil and clamor, he rose, dressed, stepped beyond the gauze bed-curtains, and asked, “What is all this noise?” Only then did the maids kneel and say, “Master, we do not know who it is, but someone outside the cave has been hurling abuse for half the night and is now battering the gate.”

p.src: The demon king left the palace gate and saw the lesser demons who had brought the report kowtowing in alarm. “Someone outside is shouting abuse and demanding Lady Golden Sage; if we say so much as half a ‘no,’ he pours out endless foul abuse, too vile to hear. When dawn came and Your Majesty still did not appear, he became so impatient that he began battering the gate.” The demon said, “Do not open the gate yet. Go and ask where he comes from, and what his surname and given name are. Return quickly and report.” The lesser demon hurried outside and called through the gate, “Who is battering the gate?” Monkey replied, “I am the maternal grandfather invited here by the Kingdom of Scarlet-Purple, and I have come to take Lady Golden Sage back to her kingdom.” On hearing this, the lesser demon reported his exact words. The demon then went to the rear palace to inquire about the visitor’s origins. The lady had only just risen and had not yet washed or dressed when a maid came to report, “Master has come.” The lady hastily straightened her clothes, loosely gathered her cloud-black hair, and came out of the palace to receive him. She had only just sat down and had not yet begun to ask questions when another lesser demon reported, “That maternal grandfather who came here has already smashed the gate.” The demon laughed and asked, “My lady, how many commanders and generals are there at your court?” The lady replied, “At court there are troops from the forty-eight guards and a thousand valiant generals; and the marshals and commanders stationed on every frontier are beyond counting.” The demon king asked, “Is any one of them surnamed Wai?” The lady replied, “Within the palace, I know only how to assist the sovereign and instruct the consorts and concubines morning and evening. Affairs outside are boundless; how could I remember everyone’s surname and name?” The demon king said, “This newcomer calls himself ‘Waigong.’ Yet as I recall, there is no one surnamed Wai in the Hundred Family Surnames. My lady, you are intelligent by nature and nobly born. Living within the imperial palace, you must have read many books. Do you remember whether that book contains such a surname?” The lady replied, “Only in the Thousand Character Classic is there the line ‘Outside, receive a tutor’s instruction.’ That must surely be the one.”

p.src: The Pilgrim laughed. “You shameless monster who deceives your sovereign and defies your king—you truly have no eyes. p.src: The demon king duly shook the first bell three times, but no fire appeared; he shook the second three times, but no smoke appeared; and he shook the third three times, but no sand appeared either. The demon king panicked. “How strange! How strange! The ways of the world must have changed. These bells are evidently henpecked: the males have seen the females, and so nothing will come out.” The Pilgrim said, “Worthy nephew, lower your hand and let me shake mine for you to see.” That splendid monkey seized all three bells in one hand and shook them together. Behold! Red fire, blue smoke, and yellow sand billowed out together, roaring as they scorched the trees and burned the mountains. The Great Sage then recited an incantation and, facing the southeast, cried, “Come, wind!” Sure enough, the wind drove the flames, and the flames rode the might of the wind. Red blaze and black murk filled the heavens with smoke and fire, while yellow sand covered the earth. Terrified out of his wits, the Great King Sai Tai Sui found every escape cut off. Trapped amid the flames, how could he possibly save his life?

p.src: Suddenly a stern voice cried from midair, “Sun Wukong, here I come!” The pilgrim hastily turned and looked upward. It was Guanyin Bodhisattva, holding her pure vase in her left hand and a willow sprig in her right, sprinkling sweet dew to extinguish the fire. Alarmed, the pilgrim hid the bells at his waist, joined his palms, and prostrated himself. The Bodhisattva flicked several drops of sweet dew from her willow sprig, and in an instant all smoke and flame vanished, leaving no trace of the yellow sand. The pilgrim kowtowed and said, “I did not know that the Great Compassionate One had descended to the mortal world, and failed to withdraw from your presence. May I ask where you are going?” The Bodhisattva replied, “I have come expressly to retrieve this monster.” The pilgrim asked, “What is this monster’s origin, that your golden person should trouble to descend and subdue him?” The Bodhisattva said, “He is the golden-haired hou that I ride. When the herdboy dozed off and neglected his watch, the wicked beast bit through its iron chain and escaped here; yet it thereby relieved the King of the Kingdom of Scarlet and Purple from calamity.” Hearing this, the pilgrim hurriedly bowed and said, “Bodhisattva, you have it backward. Here he deceived the king, abducted the queen, corrupted public morals, and brought calamity upon the king. Why do you call that relieving him of calamity?” The Bodhisattva replied, “You do not know the circumstances. When the former king of the Kingdom of Scarlet and Purple was on the throne, the present king was still crown prince and had not yet ascended the throne. In his youth he was exceedingly fond of hunting. Leading his men and horses and loosing his hawks and hounds, he came before Fallen Phoenix Slope. There, two children born to the Buddha Mother, the Peacock Wisdom King Bodhisattva of the Western Paradise—a male and female peacock chick—were resting beneath the slope. The prince drew his bow and wounded the male peacock, while the female also flew westward with an arrow in her body. After the Buddha Mother had repented, she ordained that he should suffer three years’ separation from his mate and be afflicted with a wasting illness. At that time I was riding this hou, and we both heard those words. Unexpectedly, the wicked beast took them to heart and deliberately came here to abduct the queen, thereby relieving the king of his calamity. Now three years have passed and the debt of vengeance is fully discharged; fortunately, you came to cure the king’s illness. I have come expressly to take away this evil creature.” The pilgrim said, “Bodhisattva, though that is the history of the matter, he has sullied the queen, corrupted public morals, violated human relations, and thrown the law into disorder. He deserves death for that. Now that you have personally come, his death sentence may be spared, but he cannot be spared a living punishment. Let me strike him twenty times with my cudgel before you take him away.” The Bodhisattva replied, “Wukong, since you know that I have descended to the mortal world, you should spare him entirely for my sake. It will still count as one of your feats in subduing demons. If you wield your cudgel against him, he will simply die.” The pilgrim dared not disobey and could only bow, saying, “Since you are taking him back to the Southern Sea, Bodhisattva, you must never again let him descend privately to the mortal world. The harm he has caused is no small matter.”

p.src: Only then did the Bodhisattva shout, “Wicked beast! When will you resume your true form, if not now?” The monster rolled over and revealed his original form. After he shook out his coat, the Bodhisattva mounted him. The Bodhisattva looked beneath his neck and saw that the three golden bells were missing. The Bodhisattva said, “Wukong, return my bells.” The pilgrim replied, “Old Sun knows nothing about them.” The Bodhisattva shouted, “You thieving monkey! Had you not stolen those bells, not merely one Wukong but even ten of you would not have dared approach him. Bring them out at once.” The pilgrim laughed and said, “I truly have never seen them.” The Bodhisattva said, “If you have never seen them, then let me recite the Tight-Fillet Spell.” The pilgrim panicked and cried, “Do not recite it! Do not recite it! The bells are here.” Indeed: Who was it that took the golden bells from the hou’s neck? The one who untied the bells is questioned by the one who tied them. The Bodhisattva fastened the bells beneath the hou’s neck and sprang aloft to sit high upon his back. Behold: beneath his four feet lotus blossoms blazed, while golden threads flashed thickly all over his body. The Great Compassionate One returned to the Southern Sea, of which we shall speak no more.

p.src: Now the Great Sage Sun straightened his clothes, whirled his iron cudgel, and fought his way into the Xiezhi Cave, where he mercilessly beat all the demons and monsters to death and exterminated them completely. He went straight to the palace and invited the Lady of the Sage Palace to return to her kingdom. The lady bowed to him again and again. The pilgrim related in full how the Bodhisattva had subdued the monster and the cause of the three-year separation. He found some soft grass, bound it into a grass dragon, and said, “Your Majesty, mount this, close your eyes, and do not be afraid. I shall take you back to court to see your lord.” The lady carefully obeyed his instructions. The pilgrim exercised his magic powers, and she heard only the wind rushing past her ears.

p.src: Within half an hour he brought her into the city, lowered his cloud, and called, “Your Majesty, open your eyes.” The queen opened her eyes and recognized the phoenix pavilions and dragon towers. Delighted, she cast aside the grass dragon and ascended the throne hall together with the pilgrim. When the king saw her, he hurried down from the dragon throne and reached out to take her jade-like hand, wishing to speak of the sorrow of their separation. But he suddenly fell to the floor, crying, “My hand hurts! My hand hurts!” Bajie roared with laughter and said, “Just look at him! He has no blessing to enjoy her. The moment they meet, she nearly stings him to death!” The pilgrim said, “You idiot, would you dare give her a tug?” Bajie replied, “What if I did give her a tug?” The pilgrim said, “The queen has grown poisonous spines all over her body, and her hands bear a virulent stinging poison. For the three years since she came to Qilin Mountain and lived with Sai Taisui, the monster never once touched her body. If anyone touches her body, his body hurts; if anyone touches her hand, his hand hurts.” When the officials heard this, they said, “If that is so, what can be done?” At that moment the officials outside were worried and doubtful, while the imperial consorts within were frightened. The Ladies of the Jade Sage and Silver Sage palaces, who stood nearby, helped the king to his feet.

p.src: The pilgrim went forward to greet him and asked, “Where are you going, Zhang Ziyang?” Immortal Ziyang went straight before the hall, bowed, and saluted, saying, “Great Sage, this humble immortal Zhang Boduan pays his respects.” Returning the salute, the pilgrim asked, “Where have you come from?” The immortal replied, “Three years ago, this humble immortal attended an assembly of the Buddha. Passing through this place, I saw that the King of the Kingdom of Scarlet and Purple faced the calamity of separation from his queen. I feared that the monster might violate her, corrupting human morality and making it impossible for her to reunite with the king afterward. So I transformed an old palm-fiber garment of mine into a new robe of rosy clouds that shone in five colors and presented it to the monster king, telling him to have the queen put it on as new apparel. As soon as the queen put it on, poisonous spines grew all over her body. Those poisonous spines were in fact the palm-fiber garment. Now that I know the Great Sage has succeeded, I have come expressly to lift the spell.” The pilgrim said, “Since that is so, thank you for coming from afar. Quickly release her.” The immortal stepped forward and pointed a finger at the queen, whereupon the palm-fiber garment slipped off her body. The lady’s whole body returned to its former state. The immortal shook out the garment, draped it over himself, and said to the pilgrim, “Great Sage, do not take offense. This humble immortal bids you farewell.” The pilgrim said, “Wait. Let the king thank you.” The immortal laughed and said, “There is no need, no need.” He gave a long formal bow, soared into the air, and departed. The emperor, the queen, and all the officials, high and low, hastily bowed one after another toward the sky.

p.src: When the obeisances were over, the king at once ordered the eastern hall thrown open and held a feast to thank the four monks. The king led all his people in kneeling before them, and husband and wife were at last happily reunited. In the midst of the joyful banquet, Pilgrim called out, “Master, bring out that letter of challenge.” The elder took it from his sleeve and handed it to Pilgrim. Pilgrim passed it to the king and said, “This letter was delivered by a junior officer whom the monster sent. I had already beaten that officer to death and came back to report my success. Afterward I went back to the mountain, changed into the officer, and entered the cave to make my report. Thus I was able to see Her Majesty and steal out the golden bells, though I was nearly caught by him. I transformed myself once more, stole them out again, and fought him. Fortunately, Guanyin Bodhisattva appeared and took him away, and she also told me why the peacock hen had been parted from her mate. …” He then related the whole affair in detail from beginning to end. Throughout the kingdom, among sovereign and ministers, within the palace and without, there was not one person who did not thank and praise him. The Tang Monk said, “This is due first to Your Worthy Majesty’s good fortune and second to my young disciple’s merit. Now that we have been honored with this splendid banquet, we have received more than enough. Let us take our leave here; please do not delay this poor monk’s journey west.” Unable to persuade them to stay, the king had their travel document renewed, arrayed the full imperial procession, and invited the Tang Monk to sit securely in the royal carriage. u.src: When the obeisances were over, the king at once ordered the eastern hall thrown open and held a feast to thank the four monks.
The king led all his people in kneeling before them, and husband and wife were at last happily reunited.
In the midst of the joyful banquet, Pilgrim called out, “Master, bring out that letter of challenge.”
The elder took it from his sleeve and handed it to Pilgrim.
Pilgrim passed it to the king and said, “This letter was delivered by a junior officer whom the monster sent.
I had already beaten that officer to death and came back to report my success.

Afterward I went back to the mountain, changed into the officer, and entered the cave to make my report. Thus I was able to see Her Majesty and steal out the golden bells, though I was nearly caught by him.
I transformed myself once more, stole them out again, and fought him.
Fortunately, Guanyin Bodhisattva appeared and took him away, and she also told me why the peacock hen had been parted from her mate.
…” He then related the whole affair in detail from beginning to end.

ja: きゅうちゅうないがい
u.src: Throughout the kingdom, among sovereign and ministers, within the palace and without, there was not one person who did not thank and praise him.
The Tang Monk said, “This is due first to Your Worthy Majesty’s good fortune and second to my young disciple’s merit.
Now that we have been honored with this splendid banquet, we have received more than enough.
Let us take our leave here; please do not delay this poor monk’s journey west.”
Unable to persuade them to stay, the king had their travel document renewed, arrayed the full imperial procession, and invited the Tang Monk to sit securely in the royal carriage.
The king and queen themselves held the carriage hubs and pushed the wheels, seeing him off before taking their leave.
Indeed:

p.src: As for what good or ill fortune befell them farther on their way, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
